Guthuk Noodle Soup

Served at: Losar (Tibetan New Year)

Serves 6Prep 30 minCook 1 hr

Guthuk is a traditional Tibetan noodle soup served on the eve of Losar, the Tibetan New Year. This special soup is made with hand-pulled noodles, various vegetables, and includes nine symbolic ingredients, representing good fortune and cleansing away the old year's misfortunes.

Ingredients

  • 8 cups (1.9 liters) water or broth
  • 1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour for noodles
  • 1/2 teaspoon salt
  • 1 cup (150 g) diced potatoes
  • 1/2 cup (75 g) chopped onions
  • 1/2 cup (75 g) chopped leeks or green onions
  • 1/2 cup (75 g) chopped radish
  • 1/2 cup (75 g) chopped celery
  • 1/2 cup (75 g) chopped carrots
  • 1/2 cup (75 g) chopped dried mushrooms (soaked)
  • 1/4 cup (60 ml) dried cheese curds (chhurpi) or substitute with firm cheese
  • 1/2 cup (75 g) cooked kidney beans or chickpeas
  • 1/2 teaspoon ground Sichuan pepper (optional)
  • Salt and pepper to taste
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
  • Fresh cilantro or green onions for garnish

Method

  1. In a bowl, mix the all-purpose flour with salt and enough water (about 1/3 cup or 80 ml) to make a stiff dough.
  2. Knead the dough for about 10 minutes until smooth, cover with a cloth, and let rest for 20 minutes.
  3. Roll out the dough on a floured surface into a thin sheet and cut into thin noodle strips about 1/4 inch (0.6 cm) wide.
  4. In a large pot, heat the vegetable oil over medium heat and sauté onions, leeks, radish, celery, carrots, and mushrooms until slightly softened, about 5 minutes.
  5. Add the diced potatoes, cooked kidney beans, and dried cheese curds to the pot and stir well.
  6. Pour in the water or broth and bring to a boil.
  7. Add the noodles to the boiling soup and cook for 5-7 minutes until the noodles and potatoes are tender.
  8. Season the soup with salt, pepper, and ground Sichuan pepper if using.
  9. Simmer the soup for another 10 minutes to let flavors meld together.
  10. Serve hot, garnished with fresh cilantro or green onions.

Tips

  • Traditionally, nine ingredients are used symbolizing good luck; you can adjust vegetables based on availability.
  • If you prefer, use store-bought fresh or dried noodles instead of making noodles from scratch.
  • Add a small piece of dried cheese curd (chhurpi) in each serving as a traditional touch.
